title: Bounded complete lifting from an evaluated conormal obstruction ideal
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], let $t\in A$, and suppose $A\to\varprojlim_{m\geq1}A/t^mA$ is bijective [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Let $P=A[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$ for $d\geq0$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring], let $J\subseteq P$ be a finitely generated ideal, put $B=P/J$, and let $\pi:P\twoheadrightarrow B$ be the quotient map. Write $H=H_{B/A}$ for the Gabber–Ramero obstruction ideal [def-per-gabber-ramero-obstruction-ideal], and $\widetilde H=\pi^{-1}(H)$. For $a\in A^d$, let $K(a)\subseteq A$ be the ideal generated by $g(a)$ for all $g\in\widetilde H$, where $g(a)$ is substitution into the polynomial $g$. For every integer $h\geq0$ there exist integers $r\geq0$ and $n_0>\max(r,h)$ such that for every $n\geq n_0$ and $a\in A^d$ satisfying $f(a)\in t^nA$ for all $f\in J$ and $t^h\in K(a)$, there is $b\in A^d$ satisfying $f(b)=0$ for all $f\in J$ and $b_i-a_i\in t^{n-r}A$ for every $i$. The integers $n_0,r$ may depend on $A,t,P,J,h$, but not on $n$ or $a$. No non-zero-divisor hypothesis on $t$ is imposed.

source.place: Elkik, I, Lemma 1, printed pp.555–558, principal complete Newton argument and bounded t-torsion; expressed with the conormal factorization ideal using Gabber–Ramero, Almost Ring Theory, (5.4.4) and Lemma 5.4.8, printed pp.149–150 (https://pro.univ-lille.fr/fileadmin/user_upload/pages_pros/lorenzo_ramero/releaseLNM.pdf). Agent adaptation; both archival copies WANTED. No Stacks tag is claimed for this evaluated-obstruction formulation.

proof.text: Put $T=\{z\in A:\exists m\geq0,\ t^mz=0\}$. It is an ideal: use the larger of two annihilating exponents for addition, and the same exponent for scalar multiplication. By [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], choose finitely many generators of $T$, and choose $c\geq1$ at least their annihilating exponents. Then $t^cT=0$. If $z=t^cy\in T$, some power of $t$ kills $t^cy$, hence $y\in T$ and $z=0$. Thus $T\cap t^cA=0$, precisely the torsion-separation condition in the correction lemma. For the prescribed $h$ take $r=h$ and $n_0=1+\max(2h,h+c)$. These constants are independent of both $n$ and $a$. Fix $n\geq n_0$.

source.place: Elkik I, Lemma 1, printed pp.555–556, choice of the torsion-intersection bound; direct finite-generation proof replaces the Artin–Rees invocation for this principal-ring case.

proof.text: For any tuple $u$ with $t^h\in K(u)$, write $t^h=\sum_{j=1}^s\lambda_jG_j(u)$ with $\lambda_j\in A$ and $G_j\in\widetilde H$, and put $G=\sum_j\lambda_jG_j\in\widetilde H$. Then $G(u)=t^h$. The quotient presentation is finite, so [def-per-gabber-ramero-obstruction-ideal] gives $\pi(G)\in H\subseteq H_P$ and a $B$-linear $v:B^{\oplus d}\to J/J^2$ satisfying $v\delta=\pi(G)\operatorname{id}$. Choose $g_i\in J$ representing $v(e_i)$. Apply this identity to $[f]$, using the definition of $\delta$ and of the $B$-action on $J/J^2$, to obtain $Gf-\sum_i(\partial_i f)g_i\in J^2$ for every $f\in J$. The ideals $H_P$, and thus their intersection and its inverse image, are closed under sums and scalar multiplication because their witnessing maps are; this justifies the membership asserted for $G$.

source.place: Gabber–Ramero, Almost Ring Theory, (5.4.4), printed pp.148–149, scalar-factorization characterization; agent application to an evaluated linear combination.

proof.text: Suppose $u\in A^d$ has $t^h\in K(u)$ and $f(u)\in t^qA$ for all $f\in J$, where $q>2h$ and $q-h\geq c$. With the polynomials just constructed and the torsion separation from Step 1, [lem-per-torsion-separated-newton-correction] supplies $u^+$ with $u^+-u\in(t^{q-h}A)^d$ and $f(u^+)\in t^{2(q-h)}A$ for all $f\in J$. This uses no cancellation of multiplication by $t$.

source.place: Elkik I, Lemma 1, printed pp.556–557, finite improvement (1)–(3); conormal-scalar adaptation isolated in the cited node.

proof.text: The obstruction condition persists. Polynomial evaluation preserves coordinate congruences: subtract the two evaluations of each monomial by replacing its factors one at a time. Therefore $G(u^+)=t^h+t^{q-h}w=t^h(1+t^{q-2h}w)$ for some $w\in A$. Since $q-2h\geq1$, [lem-weil-pbc-adic-complete-jacobson-radical], applied to $I=tA$, makes the factor a unit. As $G\in\widetilde H$, its value lies in $K(u^+)$; multiplying by that inverse gives $t^h\in K(u^+)$. Set $a_0=a$, $q_0=n$, and $q_{k+1}=2(q_k-h)$. Steps 2–3 and this persistence construct $a_{k+1}$ with $f(a_k)\in t^{q_k}A$, $t^h\in K(a_k)$ and $a_{k+1}-a_k\in(t^{q_k-h}A)^d$. The base is the hypothesis. Induction gives $q_k=2h+2^k(n-2h)$, so $q_k>2h$, $q_k-h\geq n-h>c$, and both exponents tend to infinity. These inequalities verify every subsequent application.

source.place: Elkik I, Lemma 1, printed p.556, successive approximations; Gabber–Ramero Claim 5.4.14, printed p.152; explicit preservation of the evaluated ideal.

proof.text: For each $m\geq1$, the residues of each coordinate of $a_k$ modulo $t^mA$ are eventually constant: once $q_k-h\geq m$, every later difference lies in $t^mA$. These eventual residues are compatible under reduction. By bijectivity in [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], they determine a unique tuple $b\in A^d$. Fix $f\in J$ and $m\geq1$, and take $k$ large enough that $b\equiv a_k\pmod {t^mA}$ and $q_k\geq m$. Evaluation in the quotient ring gives $f(b)\equiv f(a_k)=0\pmod {t^mA}$. Thus all coordinates of the image of $f(b)$ in the inverse limit vanish; injectivity gives $f(b)=0$. Finally every increment of $a_k$ lies in $(t^{n-h}A)^d$, so its eventual residue modulo $t^{n-h}A$ equals that of $a_0$. Hence $b_i-a_i\in t^{n-h}A=t^{n-r}A$. This also covers $d=0$: there are no coordinate choices, and the same evaluation and injectivity argument applies.

source.place: Elkik I, Lemma 1, printed p.556, convergence of successive approximations; explicit compatible-residue construction using the completion definition.

proof_origin.place: Elkik I, Lemma 1, printed pp.555–558, combined with Gabber–Ramero (5.4.4), printed pp.148–149; explicit conormal-scalar reconstruction, not a direct application of Elkik’s Jacobian-minor ideal.
